Notes: Grammatical: Liebermann’s “abs” or “absol” (English “absolute”) encompasses several senses. It may abbreviate absolutus in the phrase “ablative absolute” (generally for Latin expressions). Or it may abbreviate German absolut, used in the sense “im absoluten Gebrauch” (“in absolute use”), i.e. standing alone without grammatical complement or modifier: see altr[ui] (Old French), where abs. sbst. marks the use of a pronoun as a standalone substantive noun. In application to verbs, it may mark what would in modern grammatical analysis be termed an intransitive, denoting “standing alone, without object or complement”: see clamare (Latin), where abs picks out the intransitive sense “to complain”. See also earnian (Old English), and forg[ie]meleasian, in which [abs.] distinguishes an appearance of the verb used in general, predicative sense (=“is negligent”, as opposed to “to neglect [something]”).
